opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a real and growing gap between the two. Capabilities have moved incredibly fast. Models can write code, solve competition math, and hold remarkably fluent conversations. But our understanding of why they work, and especially when they'll fail, hasn't kept pace.

That gap matters because capability on a benchmark isn't the same as reliability in the world. A lot of my work has looked at robustness and distribution shift. A model can look excellent on the test set and then behave in surprising ways when the inputs change slightly, or when someone tries adversarially to break it. If we don't understand what the model has actually learned, whether it's picked up the underlying structure or some shortcut that happens to correlate with the right answer, we can't predict those failures.

What I find interesting is that understanding doesn't have to mean full mechanistic interpretability of every neuron. Sometimes it means having the right abstractions. Can we characterize how pretraining and fine-tuning interact? Can we say when fine-tuning distorts useful features versus preserving them? Can we anticipate how a model will extrapolate? Some of the most practical progress has come from those kinds of questions, where a bit of theory or careful experimentation tells you something actionable, like a better way to fine-tune so you don't lose robustness.

So I'd say the relationship should be more of a feedback loop than it is today. Right now capability tends to come first and understanding lags behind, sometimes a lot. As these systems get deployed in higher-stakes settings, closing that gap becomes essential. It's not just a scientific curiosity. It's what lets us trust these systems, fix them when they go wrong, and build the next generation in a more principled way.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes a growing gap: model capabilities have advanced quickly, while understanding why they work and when they fail has not kept pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the gap between the two has been widening, and that worries me more than it excites me.

If you look at the last few years, capabilities have moved incredibly fast. Models can write code, reason through math problems, do things we would have called impossible not long ago. But our understanding of why they work, when they'll fail, and what they've actually learned hasn't kept pace. We're building systems whose behavior we can observe but can't really predict. We train something, we run a benchmark, and we see a number go up. That tells us surprisingly little about what's happening inside.

I come at this from a robustness perspective, so the way I tend to frame it is in terms of failure modes. A model that works beautifully on the distribution it was trained on can break in ways that seem almost absurd when the inputs shift a little. And the frustrating thing is that those failures often aren't random. They reflect something the model learned, some shortcut or spurious correlation, that we didn't intend and didn't notice. Capability and understanding aren't the same axis, and sometimes they almost pull against each other. The more capable the system, the more it can mask the places where it's actually doing something fragile.

So I don't think of understanding as a nice-to-have that comes after capability. I think of it as the thing that determines whether the capability is real. If I can't tell you under what conditions a model's good behavior holds, then I don't really know what it can do. I just know what it did on the examples I happened to check.

That said, I'm not pessimistic. Part of why I find this moment interesting is that the scale of these models forces us to develop better scientific tools. You can't eyeball a trillion-parameter system. So we're pushed toward thinking carefully about what questions are even answerable, what kinds of experiments isolate a mechanism, and how to reason about behavior at a level of abstraction above the weights. That's the direction I want the field to go: treating these models as objects of study rather than just artifacts to be shipped.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities have advanced quickly while understanding why models work, when they fail, and what they learn has not kept pace.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty big gap between what we can get models to do and our understanding of why they work so well. We can train models that have really impressive capabilities, but we don’t necessarily understand when those capabilities will hold up or when they’ll fail.

And that makes understanding more than just an intellectual question. If we want to rely on these models, we need to know what happens when the setting changes, or when they encounter something different from their training data. A model doing well on a benchmark is useful evidence, but it doesn’t fully tell us what we can trust it to do.

So I see capabilities and understanding as closely connected, but not automatically moving together. Better capabilities give us new phenomena to study, and hopefully better understanding helps us build models whose behavior is more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says there is a “pretty big gap” between models’ impressive capabilities and our limited understanding of why they work so well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty striking gap between what our models can do and our understanding of why they work. We can train models that perform incredibly well on a wide range of tasks, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we understand what they’ve learned or when they’re going to fail.

To me, that makes studying their limitations especially important. If a model does well on a benchmark, what does that tell us about how it will behave when the setting changes? Which aspects of its performance are reliable, and which depend on patterns that might not hold outside the training data? Those questions connect understanding to practical usefulness. We don’t need a complete theory before we can use a model, but better understanding can help us figure out where to trust it and how to improve it.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly describes a striking gap between models’ strong performance and our limited understanding of why they work.
